No evidence was taken before the committee. The only document before the committee was the official return which has been printed and distributed amongst hon. members. Apart from that, we only had the statements of the parties concerned and of their counsel; I believe those statements were taken down and would he available if desired. It is not

It is usual for the Chairman to move, after he has presented his report, that it be taken into consideration on a future day, and it shall be placed on the Order Paper for that day. On the motion of Mr. Richardson the House went into Committee on Bill No. 28 respecting the Belleville Prince Edward Bridge Company-Mr. Porter-Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-Directors to have power to regulate tolls.

Have the tolls mentioiied in the Bill been agreed to by the opponents of the measure? I understand there was very strong opposition to this Bill from the people of Belleville and the surrounding municipalities.
Within six months.

They have six
months in which to make the purchase.
Was the price fixed?
The price was fixed in the Bill, and the bridge can be taken over at any time.
What is- the price?

The price is $72,500. The chartered accountant who was asked to look into the matter, reported that if the -estate who- own the bridge were allowed six per cent on their money, they would receive $117,000, and if allowed five per cent -the amount would be considerably less. There were certain disputes as to when the period should begin, but the amount fixed was a compromise arranged between the parties, and all those interested agreed That the increase in tolls was a fair one, and would not produce more than five per cent on the money invested.
Was Mr. Parliament, the local member for Prince Edward, a party to the arrangement?
He was a party to it.
Did he accept the tolls agreed upon, and also the price?
He did.
And the new conditions?
He accepted the price and the tolls. The ex-reeve of the municipality was also present and also agreed that the tolls were reasonable.
Then the objecting parties were satisfied?
Yes.

The hon. member for Maisonneuve has asked if Mr. Parliament attended the Committee. I do not believe he was before the sub-committee, or at the last meeting of the Committee, but he was present previously. The city of Belleville was represented by its solicitor and mayor, and the township o-f Prince Edward by Mr. Dempsey. The Sutherland estate was represented by one of the estate and by their solicitor, Mr. Kilmer. By arrangement, Mr. Clarkson, accountant, was chosen to make an investigation, and the subcommittee reported that all the interested parties had agreed, although I may say that the city of Belleville gave instructions to Mr. Pringle not to consent to anything. But we put the restriction within the Bill that within six months the municipalities would have the Tight to purchase for the sum of $72,500, and to complete the purchase within one year. So as to make the terms more convenient between the parties, the tolls, which were based on recommendations made by Mr. Clarkson, and which permit of a reasonable profit figured at five per cent to be made by the operators of the bridge, will not * 
come into force before three months from date. The object of this is to allow all parties to get together, and take advantage of the provision which was introduced into the Bill, that upon giving notice by any municipality interested in the bridge within six months it can be purchased for the sum of $72,500. Nobody was left in ignorance on the matter, everybody interested was invited to state their views, and the sub-committee reported, after all the evidence had been taken and everybody had been given a chance to present their claims.

I might further explain that the municipalities interested sent representatives to wait on the Ontario Government to see what assistance they would grant, and that government agreed to assist to the extent of at least forty per cent, with the object that the parties concerned might be able to so arrange it that the bridge would become a public work.
We may assume then that whatever objection originally existed with respect to the tolls to be charged has disappeared, in view of the compromise arranged in regard to the purchase of the bridge?
Yes.
Absolutely.
Section agreed to, and Bill reported and read the third time.

speechtext:
I hope that my right hon. friend will not persist in this motion, which has reference to the safeguards which are provided in the rules of the House with regard to Private Bills. Many of the Private Bills which come before the House affect the rights of third parties-divorce Bills, for instance, or applications for patents, which we have before us very often. All the rules mentioned in this motion safeguard the rights of third parties who may have objection to such Bills. Without going in particular into any one of these rules, let me call attention to one or two. Rule 52 says:
Every Bill shall receive three several readings on different days, previously to being passed. On urgent or extraordinary occasions a Bill may be read twice or thrice, or advanced two or more stages in one day.
If we dispense with this rule a Private Bill may be railroaded through the House and a party who may desire to present his objections to it will have no opportunity of doing so. This rule has very seldom been departed from.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: I think subsection 1 should be amended to provide that all civil servants appointed in the future should not have the privilege of voting. The Civil Service should not have the vote, but I should not like to take the vote away from any of those who *were appointed in the past when that was the law of the country. But if we now amend the Act to provide that any civil servant appointed in the future should not have the vote, then no one would have anything to complain of . because, if a person wishes to retain the vote, he need not take a position under the Government. It would be much better for the Service and for the country if the Civil Service did not have the franchise. We now propose to bring the Outside Service under this Act, and the Government is taking over a big mileage of railways and we shall have thousands and tens of thousands of officials under the Government, so that the question of this vote may be a serious one. It has been found better in the Old Country that civil servants should not vote. Very few of them now vote, and there is no doubt, if civil servants did not have the vote, we would have a better service, and there would be less politics in the Service and fewer dismissals of officials when there is a change of Government. I should like to see that subsection changed.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: It was the desire of the Government, in presenting this Bill to Parliament, to avoid the introduction of [DOT] any new matter other than was -absolutely necessary. My hon. friend's suggestion involves a very important principle, which will have to be considered some time, but I would not be disposed to view it favourably this session. When the Government, consolidates its railway interests in this country, it is probable that some provision will have to made- in respect to the railway employees voting at elections. In one of the provinces of Australia, I understand the railway employees have the right of selecting a parliamentary representative from among themselves. I do not know just what the details of the legislation are, but there is undoubtedly something to be said in its favour. For a great number of years the civil servants in England were debarred from voting; that rule was afterwards relaxed, but in the last fifteen years I understand that efforts have been made on many occasions by members of the British House ' of Commons to revert to the old rule. Ho-wever, I think it is too late in the session to take into consideration a matter of such importance.

Section agreed to.
.Mr. BUREAU: Before proceeding with the next section I would remind the minister to what took place last Saturday in connection with section 30. I took exception to that section -as not being absolutely in line with the principle of the Bill, which was to abolish the abuse of patronage, and the minister said :
Mr. A. K. Maclean: Let us pass the section, and we will revert to it later.
Mr. Bureau: How can we revert to It if we pass it?
Mr. A. K. Maclean: By consent of the committee.
Mr. Bureau : I understand that the idea is to pass the Bill to-night, and then we shall hear no more of it. If the Bill is not to pass to-

night, all right; I reserve the right, with the consent of the Government, to coijie back to this section later.
I should like to come back to this section for just a moment. The exception I took to this section on Saturday was this: During the general discussion of the principle of this Bill it was staked by every member who addressed the committee that the object was to make the Civil Service a career so that the best possible men would come into it, and with that in view, political influence was to be abolished in the matter of appointments and dismissals. I am in favour of that principle, and in favour of this Bill, hut I do not want a sham Bill, or a Bill whose pretended good effects will disappear as soon as the legislation has been prut on the statute book. The great complaint about patronage in the past has been not so much concerned with appointments as with dismissals; lor every ten lines of Hansard relating to appointments there are ten pages relating to dismissals'. I claim that if we want to make the Civil Service efficient, if we want to induce men of ability to enter it-, we must give these men some protection. Now, this section gives no protection whatever to the men who enter the Civil Service. Of course, I may be told not to think that the heads of departments are going to act in an arbitrary way. But we never know What may happen. We have seen things dqne in the last few years which we never would have dreamt of. But assuming that the head of a department or the deputy head will never *arbitrarily dismiss a man, there nevertheless remains the fear in the heart of a man who may seek an appointment that he is liable to be dismissed at the caprice of the minister or the whim of the deputy head. When I brought this question up on Saturday the minister said that he did not see how the section could be amended. The power to dismiss must remain in the Government, he said. I do not share the view of the minister. The object of this Bill is not only to control appointments, hut to show the people of this country that the Union Government is determined to carry out its promise of abolishing patronage. I understand that its object is to better the conditions o-f the Civil Service so that men of ability will be induced to devote their services to the country, that salaries will be increased, and that there will he a more careful picking of tthe best men. The Minister of Customs said on Saturday that he did not see how the section could be

amended very well. Now, I have prepared an amendment which I am going to submit to the committee. If it is rejected I shall nevertheless feel I have done my duty by trying to protect the Civil Service as far as possible. I therefore beg to move that the following be substituted for section 30:
Subject to the provisions of section 3 of this Act the power to remove or dismiss any deputy head, officer, clerk or employee shah vest in the Commission.
Before exercising such power the Commission shall require a statement in writing from the minister in the case of a deputy head, and1 .from the deputy head in all other cases, giving the causes, reasons and facts invoked for such dismissal. Upon receipt of such statement in writing the Commission shall forthwith communicate a copy of same to the deputy head or other employee whose dismissal is sought. The deputy head or employee shall within three days after the reoeipt of copy of said statement file with the Commission a statement in writing in answer to such charges, in default of which the Commission may proceed on the statement submitted' asking for dismissal.
That provides for notice being given to the man whose head is at stake that he is charged with such and such an offence, and gives him the opportunity an accused enjoys in any court of law of making answer to those charges. If the accused does not submit an answer within three days, the commission can proceed ex parte on the statement submitted asking for dismissal. I think this amendment, if adopted, will protect the civil servants; it will also serve to test whether this Bill has not been brought forward knowing that it is lame in many respects. If we are going to improve the Civil Service we want people to know that the country is willing to protect the members of the service, and we do not want to leave in the hands of a minister or deputy minister the right to dismiss an employee at will. Some one may object that section 30 does not provide for dismissal by the minister or deputy minister, but by the Governor in 'Council, but we all know how that works out. The Cabinet is now composed of twenty-three or twenty-five members, and each member has ten or a dozen commissions to supervise, as well as the legislation of his department to look after. The consequence is that when a minister comes before council with a recommendation for such a paltry thing ias the dismissal of an employee, the recommendation will not be inquired into very closely, and the minister's colleagues will let it go through as a matter of courtesy. My amendment may be voted down, but, I repeat, I have submitted it for two pur-

poses, first to protect 'Government employees and secondly, to test the good faith of those who are promoting this Bill. _

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: I do not understand why it is necessary to .suggest that the amendment is submitted to test the good faith of those who are promoting this Bill. My hon. friend, I think, is illogical there. It is quite true that the question of dismissals from the Civil Service has been more or less a political question. But the Governor in Council has never been in the habit of diemissing employees of the Inside Service; at least, I know of very few cases in which any employee of the Inside Service has been dismissed by the Government except for cause. I think that every regard has been paid to that part of the Civil Service in which appointments are made by competitive examination and promotions made upon merit. Inasmuch as the system of competitive examination and promotion by merit is to be applied to the Outside Service, I think it is not necessary to suggest that the power tof dismissal be placed in the hands of the Civil Service Commission. Many hon. members have been protesting against this Bill on the ground that it will create a powerful bureaucracy. This is carrying that idea farther. I .think it is perfectly sound to say that the phwer of dismissal should rest with the Governor in Council. Civil servants are employees of the Government, and I do not think the power of dismissal should rest anywhere except with that body. I do not think the civil servant would suffer in any respect whatever by the power resting with the Governor in Council. It is preferable that it should be there.

speechtext:
I just drafted the clause since I came into the Chamber, but I bavie thought it over. I am willing to accept any suggestion, the adoption of which will ensure the protection; of the civil servant. I do not object to the power of dismissal remaining in the Governor in. Council, but I think we should make a provision that when a minister makes a recommendation to Council fox the dismissal of a civil servant the brief of the employee answering the charges made against him should be attached to the recommendation so that the Governor in Council may have both sides. The 'hon. the Acting Minister of Finance says that I am illogical, but my position is this:	This Bill is brought before the House for the purpose of keeping a political pledge, and if so all these various clauses are useless. The pledge that was made, as shown in the Order in Council of the 13th February, 1918, and in the words of the Prime Minister was "Civil Service reform with the view of .extending the principle of the Civil Service Act to the Outside Service." I want to impress the Committee with a realization of the meaning of these words; they mean abolishing patronage. The promise was made that patronage should be abolished and that the Outside Service, as well as the Inside Service, should be brought under the Civil Service Commission. If that is all you propose to do, 1 do not see why you should pass this Act. On the other hand, if your object is to improve the Civil Service Act, I would say: Let us go into- it, make our suggestions, discuss them and see whether we cannot improve the existing Act. It has been stated by the Acting Alinister of Finance that there are only a few clauses to be changed. I think -we ought to change more if we are going to take the matter up. I believe in improving the Act, and I



believe in doing it this session. To say that we can amend the Act again next session, is no reason why we should not pass the best Bill that, in the limited time at our disposal, we can agree upon.

'Mr. G. B. NICHOLSON:	It seems to
me we would make very much more sensible progress, to say the least, in discussing a matter that deals with the whole Civil Service of Canada, embracing some seventy thousand employees, if we came down from the air and treated the whole subject from a practical point of view. Just such a step as is contemplated by the amendment was taken by some of the large corporations in this country some twenty or twenty-five years ago but it was found to be absolutely unworkable and inapplicable. The plan followed by the most successful corporations in this country in employing men is not to discourage the appointment of those who have relatives in their service, but just the reverse. They do not consider it a detriment to a man to have relatives already in their service. To my mind the amendment would bring into contumely efficient public servants just because they had in some other department of the service a cousin or a brother or a father. The whole thing is entirely out of harmony with what in my judgment should be the aim in securing an efficient public service. If the apprehensions that have been expressed on the floor of this House with regard to the deputy ministers and those in charge of departments are justified, I think it is time we set about to find a group of honest onen to place at the head of those departments. Personally it has not been either my pleasure or my misfortune to be brought into, very close touch with the cloven-hoof breed from which these men are evidently recruited if they are what they have been represented to be. If they are of that breed, we should certainly try to find means of getting rid

of them, because in an efficient public service it is necessary to have honest -men at the head of departments. I do not wish to be understood as casting reflection on these men. I have heard them referred to in commendable terms as being efficient, honest, hard-working and painstaking officials, anxious to do- their duty to their country. But to entertain the suspicion that they are constantly trying to load the public service with inefficient employees just because they happen to be their relatives is to my mind an insult. That is what the amendment is to my mind. If the men at the head of departments of the public service are so small and narrow as to be influenced by considerations of that kind, we had better get rid of them and find other men big enough to do the work.

speechtext: I do not think this amendment would have been moved had it not been- that 'several times during this year the question of nepotism has come up in this House and has caused what we might call a mild form of scandal. There is the case o-f the Auditor General, a man whom we all respect. It has heen stated in this House that he virtually compelled the commission to appoint his sons to lucrative office in the public service. The Auditor General is the man Who supervises the service of everybody in the department, and he would he a rash man, indeed, even if he weTe a minister, who would refuse him an appointment. Another case is that oi my esteemed and gallant friend, Colonel Labatt. Colonel Labatt is a man who is quite capable of standing on his own merits anywhere, but he has the political misfortune to be related by marriage to three ministers of the Crown and his case has been cited all over the country as being one of nepotism and favouritism and -sneers have been indulged in with regard to his appointment. In view of the.fact that these prominent cases have come to our attention, I think the time is opportune to take some stand with regard to the matter.

I do not object'to Mr. Fraser's son getting an appointment; he may be the very best man in Ottawa for it. I do not think this case should influence anybody but still the fact remains that it has had a certain effect upon the public mind. The suggestion is made that when the House is dealing with this matter now it would be advisable to have something put in the Act as a check, or a brake, on deputy ministers so that they would not put all of their own families into office. We are all human; everybody is human. This would not prevent a deputy minister from putting his son into a job in the service that possibly called for a very high salary, such as a position in the first division, but if the deputy minister knew that he would have to state that the man whom he had appointed was his son and that that report -would be presented to this House, he would hesitate. It is puerile to say that all this information cannot be easily obtained by the Civil Service Commission and that before a man is appointed the commission cannot ascertain whether he is the relative of any person already in the service, whether he is a Protestant, a Roman Catholic, or a member of any other religion, his age and whether married or single. To find that out does -not require a staff of 300 or 400 people. In view of the agitation which has gone out all through the country because some of these things have come to the attention of the public within the last four or five months, we should do something to avoid any complaint in the future as far as nepotism is concerned. Everybody knows that possibly 65 per cent of the deputy ministers of the Crown are either ex-members of Parliament, defeated candidates or men who have been in politics. I think they are a very efficient lot of men but my experience is that both out of office and in office they are very strong partisans. I found during the regime of the old Government that when I recommended an efficient man for appointment to the service, because he belonged to one party and the deputy minister belonged to the other, the appointee's tenure of office would only be a few months. Some excuse was found and he would be put out of his position. Those deputy ministers be-

long to the old regime. Until we create a set of deputy ministers who are neutral we will have this strong party bias manifested in the administration of the departments. The old political parties are not dead yet. There is a lot of the old Adam in people at the present time and you cannot eliminate it. Perhaps after all, it is better that we should stick to the party system because my researches in history have shown me that the only safety for the people's liberties lies in party and not in faction.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext:
I fail to see that there is anything wrong with this amendment. I have not heard any strong argument why such an amendment should not be passed, and I think some very forcible arguments have been presented why it should be passed. There is no doubt that in the public mind the idea is that nepotism and favouritism exist; that is the putting into positions, 'sometimes with large emoluments, of people who have nothing to recommend them except the pressure and influence exerted by their friends. It is no doubt true that in the city of Ottawa there are many families who have extraordinary advantages, in that members of these families have been placed one after another in positions in the Civil Service. Living next door to a widow with a couple of girls who have no influence, no one to go and put in a word for them, you may find a family with six or seven members in the Civil Service and another one growing up and also getting into the Civil Service, while the widow and her two children have no chance whatever. It is all very well to say that this is done by examination. Of course it is, but the fact remains that one can bring pressure and influence to bear and the other cannot. I do not say that necessarily the commission would be unduly influenced, but, as the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) says, we are all human. The principle of the amendment offered by the hon. member for West Toronto is something that this House and the country can understand. What wrong will be done by giving the lever to the Civil Service Commission that this amendment will give, and enabling it to say, when somebody -wants to get a position, "It is true you have passed the examination, but here is a person who has also passed the examination; you have six members of your family in the service already; you cannot get the position." It is about time that somebody took hold of the affairs of the country along the line which the amend-

ment suggests, so that favouritism shall be *abolished.
What do to hear every day from the military service point of view? The cry is put up: This family has two hoys gone to the front, you should not .take the last one. By analogy I would like to see-when a family has been well taken care of in the Civil Service by a number of its members being employed,-the same principle act in the opposite way, and have it declared: You shall not go into the Civil Service, because there has been enough done by the country for your brothers and sisters.
I find myself in this matter desirous of corroborating the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken), because to my knowledge, obtained in a casual way, there is a great abuse in the practice which is aimed at and sought to be stopped by this amendment. It does seem to me that unless some sound reason to the contrary is furnished, the amendment should be adopted. It does not do merely to say that because certain persons are competent to do the work, that therefore they should he appointed. I am assuming the competency of ten members of a family, but I do not see why those ten persons should be given positions when there are other persons standing by who ought to be chosen, who are equally competent, who have passed the necessary examination, but are not able to get a hearing before the powers that he- they have not got the aggression or knowledge of the way to go about it,-and, therefore, they suffer.

It seems to me that we should not worry about the possible effects of this amendment. It is not going to interfere with any appointments that are being made, it is not going to prove a bar to the appointment of even relatives. Hon. members who have studied the Civil Service, and know anything about the condition of affairs, will agree with me that we ought not to be too delicate about hurting the feelings of civil servants in this country. We have had whole families living at the public crib; sisters, cousins, and aunts, have all piled in. The average member of Parliament knows nothing about this, but it is an absolute fact. The amendment of the member for Toronto is only designed to guard against a certain state of affairs, and to protect the public and the Civil Service itself. As I said, it is not going to prove any bar to the appointment of any person to the Civil Service, but the amendment embodied in the Act will be a deterrent to deputy
ministers and to other civil servants, and through its agency we will probably put a check upon nepotism. Those of us who know anything about the conduct of the Civil Service know that nepotism has been rampant in the country for the last thirty or forty yeare. We need not worry aboht whether there is a precedent for our action or not. This is a Union Government, composed of, and supported toy, two parties, and it can afford to establish precedents. What do we care about British or other traditions in connection with this matter? We are trying to do the best we can for the people, and God knows they need some service at the present time. If, by the introduction of this amendment, we can prevent nepotism and assist the people of the country in saving a little money, by all means let us adopt the amendment.

I, for one, am assuming that the Civil Service Commission is composed of honest and honourable men. If they are, I cannot understand why we should clutter up their report with the names of aunts, cousins, brothers, sisters or any other relatives that .may be in the service of the country. If there is an application from a person to be appointed to the Civil iService, and he is not qualified, having a brother or a cousin already there is not going to get him into the service. speechtext: The remarks I made this morning upon a previous amendment *apply equally to the present one, and I *have been wondering whether the mover of the present -amendment has really considered what it means. In my opinion, the thing is absurd. Take my own case, for instance. My wife has sixty first cousins, and I have about thirty. Besides, there are uncles and aunts, and grandfathers and grandmothers.

I did not have the good fortune to hear the discussion on this *question this morning, as I was attending the sittings of a committee of the House, buit I can see very little abjection to the amendment which has been offered. We were given to understand that one of the objects of the Bill was to do away with the influence that might be exerted in securing appointments. Now, we are told that it would be a reflection on some people if lists of their relatives were published.
I have -been in public life, more or less, for sixteen years-including service in the provincial as well as the Federal House- and during that time, so far as 'I know, not one relation of mine, either by blood or marriage has occupied a position in the service, of either the province or the Dominion. Therefore, I am not as sensitive *about publication in this matter as some other gentlemen may be. There is a suspicion in the minds of the people, and it is useless trying to ignore it, that friends of the Government have received favours in-
directly at the hands of those who have a right to recommend appointments. You cannot pick up a newspaper these last few days without reading a reference to something of the kind. I think the amendment is a very good one, and it will tend to check anything of that nature. I regret that it should be necessary to provide such safeguards, but I have no more confidence in the Civil Service Commission than I have in a great many other people, and for that reason I do not see any reason why the light of publicity should not be flashed upon -every appointment made to the Civil Service in Canada.

As my hon. friend from Edmonton has said, there will be nothing to prevent the appointment of nine or ten members of the same family provided they pass the required examination. The amendment will not remedy the evil complained of. As to the evil of nepotism in the Civil Service and its elimination, I agree entirely with the hon. gentleman, but it should be made a matter of a special amendment, as it is in the American Civil Service Act. There is a -section in that Act providing as follows :
9. That whenever there are already two or more members of a family in the public service in the grades covered by this Act, no other member of such family shall be eligible to appointment to any of said grades.

You would not require anything of the kind, Mr. Chairman. Here is a point I would like to submit to the House. I have never found any objection on the part of any man to the widest publicity if he has done anything that he can defend, Now, whether we are going by this Act to establish a system that will result in a very serious degree of nepotism can only be ascertained from the information we wsuld get in this report. As the Civil Service stands to-day you can go over the Civil Service list with some person in the service familiar with it, and pick out a great many cases where there are four or five, or half a dozen or more, of the same family in the service. To make an investigation of that kind would be an exceedingly difficult thing to do, and take months to complete. But if we get a report such as I am suggesting every year we would be able to tell each year how far this practice of nepotism is getting into the " service. If it is not getting into any degree which seems to us to be dangerous, that ends it. If it is getting in, we will have the information in such a way that we can see it at a glance. If that happens-and we are making it a possibility under this Act, Mr. Chairman-and we discover it in the first, or the second, or the third year, then this House will take some action to put an end to it. Unless it has that information the House cannot proceed at all. 1 submit there is no other way, no better and no cheaper way. The acting minister says this will take one large volume, perhaps two. That only proves my case, because if they are going to make so many appointments that it will take two or three volumes to print the names of their relatives already in the service we ought to know it. I do not think there is any information that will be more desirable or interesting to this country than would be contained in those two or three volumes. If the cost will be as great as to require the [DOT] printing of two or three volumes, it would

be necessary for this House to take some action at the next session of Parliament.

Then why does my hon. friend want the information? Appointments to the public service are not to be viewed as favours; they go to those who receive them as a matter of right, on their

merits and qualifications as disclosed by the examinations. If that be the case, why should we inquire whether one, two, or a dozen members of the same family aie in the Civil Service? If the principle of examination and competition is to prevail- and that is professedly the very essence of this measure-surely we do not need to inquire how many relatives the candidate has in the public service. Reference has been made to the' Auditor General. I have not looked into his case; I only know that he Is an able and faithful public official. But i-f any son or daughter of the Auditor General submitted himself or herself for examination and won the prize legitimately, why should he or she not receive the appointment? 1 Is the member for West Toronto not defeating the whole purpose and intention of this Bill in the amendment which he hias submitted? True, he does not say that you must not appoint more than one or two members of the same family, hut if his amendment does not mean that, what is the object of getting all this information, of investigating family trees and holding these inquests from ocean to ocean? If the principle of this Bill is not that of establishing a system of open, free, public competition, then, as a distinguished statesman once said, " There hain't nothing to it." Let men be appointed simply on merit, regardless of colour, creed, politics, or relationship.

. Sir 'GEORGE FOSTER:	Before that
amendment is put to the vote. I want to express my own view in reference to it and to call the attention of the committee to what seems to he involved. In the first place, when the amendment was read, it grated upon my feelings as a citizen of a united country. It seems to me that the principle - involved in this tends to cut us off into, provincial sections, to can us in sectional compartments. It therefore puts up a barrier against the free currency of the service and the talent of the whole country as devoted to the work of the whole country. It seems to me that it tends to cultivate provincialism rather than nationalism. _ What reason in the world is there why a' man who is born in British Columbia and has talents and capacity should not have an opportunity of serving in the public service in any part of Canada? From my point of view that seems to be the broad ground upon which we should develop. If,
on the other hand you make a regulation by which you virtually say that no one but a British Columbian shall be allowed to act in the service of the Dominion in British 'Columbia, no one but a Quebec man shall be allowed to act in the public service anywhere in Canada except in Quebec, and so on throughout all the provinces, you rather bar the current of communication, sympathy, active service and nationality. I do not think there is any better basis than that the appointments which are to he made by the Civil Service Commission will be made for the good of the service. I should think that it would be the inevitable tendency that for the larger proportion of the offices there would be sufficient material in the different localities of the different .provinces to look after the public service in those localities. As an illustration of my contention, let me say this: Two years ago, when I was proceeding by water to the extreme northern limits of my constituency, about four hundred miles from Edmonton, we found a chief fire ranger sent from Ottawa. I will give a concrete instance showing that the folks in Ottawa are not willing to play the fair game with us. A young lady came from France not very long ago with her brother and sister. subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: I stand on that ground to-day. To say that the riding I have the honour to represent, or that some other member may represent, cannot supply the men or women to fill any jobs in that constituency is belittling, and this belittling of our own people is becoming too much the custom in Canada to-day. We have thousands of men and women in our constituencies able to fill any job. Why is it necessary for any one in British Columbia or Nova Scotia to he sent to fill a job in Northumberland, or vice versa? Every person required to fill a constituency job should be furnished hy the constituency. If there is a position to be filled in a province, let it be filled from the province; or if the position is a federal office, let it then be advertised all over Canada and get the best man. So far as competitive examinations are concerned, I do not know whether the clause dealing with them is passed or not, but I trust that the committee will bear in mind what was said in this regard by the hon. member for South Toronto th? other night: that a competitive examination is not a test of fitness at all. I have observed-and any minister or ex-minister who ever had anything to do with the Civil Service will agree-that those who have not passed examinations are the best officers in the department. This principle, particularly as applied to post office appointments, has been recognized in the United States, where the eligibility of applicants is restricted to those living in the vicinity of the town, city or county where the appointment is to he made. Another portion of this statement says:
Heretofore permanent appointment in the Inside Service was based solely on the result of an educational test (the candidate being otherwise suitable, of course, as to age, health, character and habits). This gave to the candidate fresh from the class room, and yet lacking in experience, a great advantage over the educated and altogether more suitable person who possessed business experience but might be a trifle rusty in some of the subjects written at the examination.

A great deal may be said in favour of the amendment and a great deal against it; but I am disposed to accept it, with some slight alteration. This Act departs very radically from the present Civil Service Act and it is important that it be accepted by the people. speechtext: Accepting as correct the minister's assertion that the Inside Service is confined to Ottawa, I am prepared to concur in his suggestion. I should be the last in the world to cause him the slightest feeling of discomfort, because I have the greatest respegt,for him. I regret that he looked upon my resolution in the way he did, because I did not intend it to he provincial; I merely considered it my duty to look after my constituency and my province. British Columbia has I think sent about ten per cent of her total population to the war, and the people of that province are entitled to some consideration. When it is said that we should be national, not provincial, may I point out that in this august legislature and departments connected with it, in responsible positions you will not find one person from British Columbia? I move to amend section 41, paragraph 3, as follows:	By

of the said section. That will put the Government Railway system under the Civil Service Act. I want to direct the attention of the Acting Minister of Finance to the Prime Minister's promise, and also to the Order in Council which bears upon this question and which reads:
Pending the enactment of the necessary legislation hereinbefore alluded to, the following rules shall be observed in all departments of the Government in respect to appointments to the public service.
The capitalization of the word " all " is my point. The intention of the Order in Council was to include all " services, including the Government railways, in the Civil Service. As I pointed out before, it is most important that the Government railways be brought under the Civil Service Act at this time, because, although the number of present employees runs into some thirty thousand, this is only small comparatively with the number of civil servants 'there will be in the employment of the Government railways when the Government has taken over what it now com templates. The 'Government has already taken over a part of the Transcontinental from Quebec to Winnipeg, and when it shall have taken over 'the balance of the road from Winnipeg to the Pacific, and when it shall have taken charge of the Canadian Northern railroad, as I understand the Government is about to do, we Shall have a tremendous army of civil servants who will make it difficult for any Government to pass a Civil (Service Reform Bill that will apply to them. There will be such a large number of people engaged in one service that we will have a railroad despotism in this country. It must be remembered that Canada is a very narrow country, relatively to the way it is peopled, and when we have a railway fr-m the Atlantic to the Pacific with all its branches and ramifications we will have a condition of things that hon. gentlemen would be well advised to protect themselves against while they have the opportunity. Otherwise, these organizations will be a menace to any Government in this country They will be a dominating force in politics, unless they are eliminated entirely from politics, and the only way to eliminate them from polities is to eliminate patronage, and the only way to eliminate patronage is to put the railway employees under the Civil Service Commission, and the time to do it is now, before they get big enough to dominate any Government of this country. If any more amendments are necessary beyond the one I have submitted,
to satisfy the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers, or any other railway brotherhood we can incorporate them in the Bill.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext:
I wish to support the amendment of my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Read). I see no reason why railway employees should not 'be placed under the Civil .Service Commission the same as any other branch of the public service. No good reason has been given why that should not be done. It is this department more than any other that has suffered from patronage in the province from which I come. The Intercolonial railway has been abused by the patronage system to a certain extent from the time it was first built, and I think it would be a great reform if we could get rid of the patronage evil in connection with the Government railways in Eastern Canada. The fact that every young man who applies for a position as telegraph operator, cleaner, brakesman, and what not, has to bring with hiim a certificate from a member of the patronage committee or from a member of Parliament shows that the whole system is permeated by patronage. The man who is selected in that way may TJ.'.t prove suitable.

Mr. NESBITT; How would my hon. friend get over the difficulty caused by the delay in the 'Civil Service Commission appointing >a fireman, we will say, who was required immediately?

speechtext: Regulations could be made to meet that case.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext:
I am not proposing that that class of employee should be put under the board. I iam urging that the superintendents and shop foremen should have power to select their employees in the same way that the superintendent of an industry has power to select his men. Under the present patronage system a man may be sent into the round-house who will never make a cleaner or a driver, but the superintendent cannot dismiss him like the .superintendent of an industry can dismiss any one whom he thinks will not prove suitable for the work. If the superintendents and foremen had this power they would be able to gather together a good stafh hut when men are 'appointed promiscuously under the patronage system it is impossible to get a good staff, and that is one of the reasons why the Government railways have not been successful in the past. Here is the opportunity to get rid of that difficulty and to put the road under proper management. Employees of railways may be divided into two classes, the clerical staff, who could be selected on competitive 'examination by the .Civil Service Commission, and the operating staff, who, of course, could not be selected by the Civil Service Oommiss'cn, but could rery well be appointed by the men in charge of the round-houses and the superintendents of the road. If we would give these men power to select their employees, and make them responsible for the character of the men they select, it would remove the difficulty at once. Announce that it is not necessary for applicants to get a recommendation from the patronage committee or from any member of Parliament; that the superintendents have a free hand in selecting the men they will train for engineers, conductors, and other posts in the railway service, and the whole difficulty will he solved as far as that branch of the railway is concerned. The- Minister of Public Works has already accepted this system, and who will say there should he any difference in this respect between the Government railways and the Department of Public Works? The Department of Public 'Works consists of a large number of men 
employed in manual labour .and other kinds of work. They also have in that department engineers and men who' ought to submit themselves to examination. I cannot see any material difference between the Department of Public Works and the Department of Railways and Canals as to the application of this Act. I trust that the minister will accept this amendment. This is one of the most important clauses in the Bill. If we are to have Civil Service reform in this country, it will only be a half measure unless it applies to the Government railways the same as to other departments.
'Mr. RICHARDSON:	I think it would
be a great mistake to accept the amendment of the hon. member for Prince, P.E.I. (Mr. J. Read). I presume that both the hon. piember who proposed that amendment and the hon. member for Guysbor-ough (Mr. Sinclair), who supports it, have read the report of the Drayton-Acworth Commiiseion. The commission proposes that several of the most important railway systems in the country shall be placed under Government ownership. We now own the Canadian Northern, we have the Intercolonial, we shall have the Transcontinental and we cannot avoid taking over the Grand Trunk Pacific; so that we will have a great system of railways owned by the people. The Drayton-Acworth report which,
I assume, is acceptable to the Government' and to the country, proposes that all the Canadian Government railway systems shall be placed under the control and management of an independent commission composed of the best and most practical men that money can secure. These commissioners will be responsible, not to the Government hut to Parliament, so that their independence may :be absolutely guaranteed. If you are to place the employees of the Intercolonial railway under the Civil Service Commission you will be taking these people away from the control of the commission that it is proposed to establish.
If the Government fails to appoint this commission after it has secured, control of these railways it will make a mistake that the country will never recover from. That is the only possible way by which -a national railway system can be made a success.
If you are to place the employees of the Intercolonial under the control of the Civil Service Commission, you will deprive us of the opportunity of placing them under the control of the proposed railway commission that will be appointed to manage the national railway system.

speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Richardson) is aware that the Draytonr Acworth report has been'before this House for two years and that it has not been acted upon. The Government appointed that commission at very great cost to the country; the commission travelled from one end of the country to the other and engaged specialists and technical experts to examine the railway situation. We then took cognizance of the report. It had been discussed day in and day out in this House, but the Government has discarded the report absolutely. There is a commission sitting in Toronto to-day because of the discarding of that report, and as a result of the legislation that was passed during last session. 'Therefore, my hon. friend may be quite sure that there is no hope that the Government will ever take any action based on that report which is a most excellent one. I have neveT read a report so complete and so sane as regards the Canadian railway question. Yet the Government has discarded it. My hon. friend says that the railway officials and employees of this country ought to be under the Canadian Railway Commission. Ottawa, of the qualifications -for tTairn despatcher, locomotive engineer, conductor, or any other class of men employed in the operation of railway trains? On section 42-Computation of number of probable vacancies-soldiers to have preference:

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: There is one point to which I would like to direct the attention of the minister. This section speaks of overseas soldiers and does not discriminate. There are soldiers in Canada, as I pointed out in this House not very long ago, who from the very outset have been anxious to go to the front, and who could not possibly be permitted to go. This section would militate against these men, and would put a premium upon a class of men who are no more deserving than are they, although all may be deserving. I should like to see the soldiers classified into combatants, or those who faced the foe in the field, and those who have been in Britain in offices since the beginning of the war. That is the distinction which I wish to direct the attention of the minister to, and I hope he will take it into consideration. There are men by the hundred in Britain -good fellows, I am not saying one word against them; they are doing very useful work-who have not been to the front or in the firing line at all, and who are not as much entitled to consideration as are many of the boys who were desirous of going to the front but who have remained in Canada occupying positions against their own wishes. The minister is doing an injustice, unintentionally, of course, to that class of soldier, and he is hardly putting the premium on the combatant fellow that I would like to see put on him. My heart always warms up to the fellow who faces the music ini the trenches.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext:
At the suggestion of the Acting Finance Minister, I withdrew the second amendment to section 41, and I now move it as an amendment to section 42. It is as follows:
That section 42 he amended by adding at the end of paragraph (a) of subsection 2 the following- words:
Provided also that the Commission may, in the case of any such person, decide that it is not expedient to require such person to pass the said examination and' may, without such examination, place such person on the said list of successful candidates in such order of merit as they may deem advisable.
"Person" herein referred to is set out in paragraph (a) of this section as meaning any person who has been on active service overseas on the military or naval forces of His Majesty or of any of the Allies of His Majesty during the present war. Men who have served in the overseas forces should be placed in a different position from that
occupied by ordinary individuals so far as examinations are concerned. In proper cases-of which the commission will be the judges-it is only right that returned soldiers should be so placed on the list without being required to take the examination. There is nothing unusual about that. In British Columbia in my own profession it has been decided in a great many cases by the Benchers to dispense altogether with intermediate and even with final examinations in the case of men who have served overseas. Such men are given their degrees without examination. The Civil 'Service Commission should give every consideration to the men who have fought our battles at the front. If, therefore, we place returned soldiers in a more favourable position than we place civilians, it will not be doing too much for them.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: Thousands of men have gone from Canada, have used the uniform to enable them to keep from getting within sound of the guns, have remained in England and through political influence have secured high positions there. If this amendment is passed as it is worded, these men, when they return, will be able to use the same political influence that kept their skins safe when they were in England in order to get high positions here in the Service without passing an examination. I object most strongly to that. If my hon. friend will make his amendment apply only to men 'who' have gone across the channel and fought in the trenches, I will support it, hut I protest against these political soldiers, who took good care not to get in line with the bullets, being given any special advantage over anybody else when they come home.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: And age does not count against them.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext:
That is so. It is dangerous to suggest to the commission that we want them to appoint men without regard to merit or (qualifications. The use of the

word "may" suggests that the commission "shall;"! think that we should not adopt an amendment of this kind. I agree with the Acting Minister of Finance that any favouritism which is shown should be extended to those who have seen actual service at the front. I. should not like to say anything against the men who- have gone to England with -the intention of fighting. As the member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) says, some of them may have exercised political influence to keep them from danger, but I am not saying anything about that; I am not making any insinuations. As the section is worded, it gives- returned soldiers a distinct preference. The examination- will not be a -serious matter to these men; besides, as I have said, it would 'be dangerous for -us to -suggest to the commission that they select for appointment men without merit-I mean, not individual merit, no-t the merit of having served overseas, but the merit which qualifies them for a Civil Service position. If, therefore, the section is so worded as to -give preference to the men who have seen -actual service in the trenches, I think it will be all right.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: I am very much interested in this soldier problem, and I wish to tell hon. members that I never saw a soldier who went overseas for the money that was in it or who came -back with the idea of getting a job which he was not fit to hold. I am very strongly opposed to the amendment. If returned soldiers are not competent to hold the positions, they do not want to take them, and we do not want to put them into- those positions. We do not want to make paupers of them. If we have to take care of the returned soldiers, we shall do it in some other way.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext:
This amendment is one which might lead a person who opposes it, and who- is not in the position of my hon. friend (Mr. Andrews), to be criticised and sniped at hereafter. This Bill is brought down for the purpose of rendering the 'Civil Service more effective and- improving conditions as- they now exist. I see a number of difficulties if we are going to begin to create classes by exceptions, as is suggested by the amendment of the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie). In presenting his amendment he cites a precedent; he says that in hie province-I conclude he is a lawyer-the bench in the case of men who have served overseas exempts from examination students or those who are preparing to practice the legal profession. I do not 6ee the connection be-
[Mr Nesbitt.]
tween exempting a lawyer from examination and exempting from examination a man who has gone into the Civil -Service. After a man receives his diploma or his certificate to practice as a lawyer, he hangs out his shingle; and if he can make good, that is all right. If he cannot, he has to suffer for the favour which was intended to be done to him and which did not turn out as he expected. In this case, I think the amendment as moved by the Acting Minister of Finance goes the limit. We say: You shall pass qualifying examinations. For the protection of the service,, we all admit that they are necessary. We tell the soldier:	"You deserve consideration at
the hands of the people, -and we are willing to give it to you; supposing there are fifteen candidates, and by -marks there are fourteen ahead of you, you are qualified to hold a position, but the superior qualification which you get for having risked your life for your country gives you the preference over the fourteen others who, under ordinary circumstances, would have been ahead of you -and w-ould ihave set you back." Let us take the argument of my hon. friend fro-m Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff). Supposing we are going to make differences between those who went across the channel and those who -did not, and between those who went into the trenches .and those who did not, there may be -men who- went overseas for the purpose of going into the trenches, -but who, from circumstances beyond their control, were -unable to reach the trenches. They may have been sick; they may have been under conditions which prevented them from reaching the trenches. It may have been decided that their services on one side of the channel were of more benfit than on the other. The same thing -may apply to a man acro-s-s -the channel Teady to go into the trenches. lie may become sick, or, on -account of circumstances beyon-d his control, he -may not be able to reach the trenches. An injustice would -be worked to such a man. Those are some of the objections and difficulties which we m-ay have to meet if we -accept the amendment according to -the suggestion of the hon member for Assiniboia. I agree with the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. -G. W. Andrews) that we ought not to jeopardise in any way the Bill that is now before us and which we are going to make law. We might render a bad service to the soldier himself. Supposing by mishap -a man unqualified should be put into a position, that would create a certain fee-ling against that man. It would

tend to take away from that particular man the sympathy to which he is entitled, and we ought not to expose any one to that condition.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: I quite agree with the remarks that have been made by some hon. gentlemen to the effect that we must take the greatest interest in the welfare of the returned soldier. Nobody, I imagine, would dispute that. This country must see to it that the soldier who has performed services across the seas is properly cared for, but when it is proposed to empower the commission to appoint returned soldiers to competitive posts without examination I must say I am not prepared to agree. 'Section 41 enables the commission to declare that the Act shall not apply to certain positions where its application would not be practicable, and positions of that class will be open to returned soldiers. Section 42 also gives preference to returned soldiers by enabling the commission to put them ahead-if they pass the examination-of all other candidates qualifying. That is a distinct preference. The age limit has also been removed in the case of returned soldiers, so I think hon. gentlemen will agree that same preference has been shown to this class of the community. It is rather a serious thing to suggest that appointments should be made to the Civil Service without examination of any kind. We must have a Civil Service in this country; it should be an efficient one, and I should not like to see power placed in the hands of the commission or any other body to wholly eliminate examinations for any one class. I hope this view will prevail with the committee, and particularly with the hon. member for New Westminster, who I hope will withdraw his amendment.

speechtext: Very frequently the defeated candidate has the power of recommendation.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext:
I am not complaining about that. I am not speaking of the de-ifeated candidate, but of the man who represents the people. Do not let me be misunderstood. I am not talking of cases (where recommendations are not to be made, but I say that where a recommendation has to toe made, ,and the power to make that recommendation is taken out of the hands of the people, it is a direct insult to the people's representative for one thing, and a violation of the constitution for another. There is no guarantee whatever that the appointment will be worth the paper it is written on. Furthermore-I do not wish to be insulting-it looks to me as if the deputy ministers, being amenable to nobody except the minister and having all power in their hands, will hand that power over to the minister so that the power of recommendation will be taken out of the hands of the people where it rests now with more or less satisfactory results, and will be centralized in the bands of the Government. And pray, since when has the Government had a greater moral right to say who shall be recommended than the members of this House? If the members here are not gentlemen of common decency, fit to bear the

responsibility cast upon them, or if they fancy for one minute that they can sidestep that responsibility or are not capable of making an honest recommendation, then for Heaven's sake let them resign and let some decent men take their places. 'But to suppose that the standard of representative life in this country has fallen so low that some person or persons unknown may recommend appointments! in a constituency, avoiding as if he were the plague the representative of that constituency, is to suppose something that the House and the country will not accept. You may pass this Bill, but the House and the people will not pass it and it never will go.

In view of the statement made by the acting minister a few days ago, that this Bill was considered to a certain extent more or less as a temporary measure, and that amendments would probably be brought down after it had been tried out, I think I can safely withdraw the proposed amendment. I hope, however, that next session the minister, and some other hon. gentlemen, will have changed their ideas and that they will finally decide to support this amendment. I feel that it is only a proper one and although I must agree with the remarks of hon. gentlemen to the effect that we do not want to have anyone in the Civil Service who is not capable of carrying out the duties of his office, I still think that men from the front should Ibe given different consideration from others. speechtext: Is it intended to determine the qualifications of candidates by examination and that alone? I could name a great many instances where a man might fall down on a written examination and yet be the best man for the position because he would probably have more practical experience and ability. subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: May I ask the acting minister why there is a restriction that persons not British subjects can be admitted to the Civil Service? The other night the question was raised by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) about having the oath of allegiance included in the oath to be taken by a civil servant. I understood the purpose was to make It impossible for a man to apply for a position unless he was a British subject. In this section it is provided that a man not a British subject can be appointed on the authority of the Governor in Council. I do not see how any case may arise, unless that of an interpreter, or under very extraordinary circumstances, in which a person who is not a British subject will be required to fill a position in the Civil Service.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: The purpose of this section is to enable the Governor in Council, under special circumstances, to employ the services of one not a British subject because he possesses some special knowledge upon a certain subject. For instance, two or three years ago the services of a distinguished Norwegian were secured by the Government in connection with our fisheries, and he remained in the service for a year or more. He has since ceased his connection with the Civil Service. I understand that a little difficulty would have been experienced in employing such a person were it not for this section, which is intended to cover cases of that kind.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: How does the acting minister justify the provision of only $600 a year for messengers, porters, sorters and packers? This is another case where the under dog is 'being neglected. I have talked with the messengers about here from time to time, and I find that a quiet feeling of-
