speechtext: Unrest.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend calls it " unrest." At any rate, in these days, when we talk of billions with a glib tongue, and with the price of bacon running up to 50 cents and 60 cents per pound, it is hard to understand how a messenger who has a wife and five, six, or seven children to support can get along on $600, $700, or $800 a year. Let ns get a little democracy into this enactment. How can the Government justify paying a messenger who is 
married and has four or five children, $600 a year?

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: As a matter of fact, I would think that messengers who had been married and been in the Service for a number of years would probably be getting the higher salaries. The salary of $600 would be paid to the young boy or young man, most likely unmarried, on entering the service.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: And the returned soldier. I see some of the recently appointed employees are returned soldiers. Are you going to istart men who have fought for their country at $600? What I protest against is that the rule should be hard-and-fast. When there are so many positions to be filled, a man who has fought the battles of his country is going to ask for a decent job at a decent wage, and the country wants to give that to him. If a man has been in the service for some time and has not fought for his country, he gets $1,200; but a man from the front, crippled, perhaps gassed, but still fit to do an honest year's service, should be given $1,000 a year, and you should not let him wait for the period of his death to reach up from $600 to $1,000 by the grace of somebody. The point I wish to impress is this: If you do not do it in any other way, do not fix the minimum at $600, but start at $900.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: We can start at $800.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: This is a difficult Bill to understand, but I see $600 set as the minimum. \I see some of these returned soldiers upstairs. They are bright young men; they have gone through the agonies of war, and yet they are employed by a grateful country at a salary-unless the commission has its attention drawn to the matter-of $600. It is not fair. Far too much attention is paid in this country to the fellows getting $5,000, $7,000, $10,000 a year and too little to the man who has fought for his country.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: Without joining issue with my hon. friend in any respect, I may say that under section 12 there is a possibility of appointing a man in that grade at an increase of $200 above the minimum.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext:
I quite agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Morphy). I do not think Canada is so nearly dead broke that we need ask any man to work for less than $800 a year, and a man who works for less than $800 a year is not worth very much, unless, he is driven to take such a position. Some

years ago I had the handling of what is called the "patronage" in the constituency of Regina, and in that connection it was my duty to recommend many men for positions , in the post office and other places. There are quite a number of those officers who start at $725 a year, and I have never yet succeeded in getting a good man at that salary. Those men would quickly tell me that they could make more money than that by working on the streets of Regina, and that is true. We had to accept a poor class of men, and we endeavoured to make good men by taking a poor class and gradually working them up into permanent positions. I would like to see a minimum salary fixed of not less than $800 a year to start with in all the services in the Dominion.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext:
It is not necessary for those men to start at $600. In grade C, $600 to $1,000, it is in the discretion of the commission to say what the salary shall be. There are in the Service certain branches in which young men may be employed who might very well be started at $600, and then they would be receiving more money than they could earn in other walks of life. For instance, boys in the banks do not start at $600. Boys who go into the retail mercantile service or even the wholesale mercantile service do not start at $600; they have to work up. As my hon. friend (Mr. Cowan) has said, he has often recommended people to take positions, and they would rather work at some other job than take those positions. There is nothing to compel any of those persons to accept positions in the Civil Service. This leaves it optional with the commission to say what salary shall be paid, and I have no doubt, in the case of men who have been overseas, no commission will ask them, if they are capable of filling the position to which they are appointed, to start at $600 a year. There are in the Civil Service many positions in which people are well paid,-and think they are well paid-at $600. I remember at one time a very young man, who was drawing $800 a year in one of the departments, applying to me to see if I could not get him a raise. In answer to a question he told me he had held his position for a year. I knew for a fact that, although he was a capable young man, he could not possibly command that salary in the banking or mercantile service anywhere in Canada. He was being better paid than he would be in any other walk of life that I knew of. He was anxious enough, when he first got the position, to accept it at $800 a year. If it was necessary
for everybody to start at $600, I would quite agree with my hon. friends that the minimum should be increased, but $600 might be quite acceptable in regard to certain positions in the service.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext:
That is all right, but the service itself is suffering. There are in the Regina post office some sixteen vacancies, and men cannot be got to fill them, and girls will not accept the salaries paid by the Government. The result is that business is not being done, and that unless we are prepared to start those
9 p.m. young men at higher salaries we shall not get them at all, with the cost of living and everything else increasing as it is. The minimum salary should be much higher than it is.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: I quite agree with the hon. gentleman who advocated making the minimum salary more than $600. Such a salary is a shame. There has been some sacrifice entailed in the education of any young man, however young he may be, and in large centres, such as the city of Montreal, any labouring man receives more than $600,-it is not even the wage of an apprentice at the present time. The Government should reconsider the matter so far as the big centres are concerned, where it costs so much to live. Generally speaking, those young men are supporting their mothers or fathers. Why say that a young man should not, because he is young, be paid.just as much As a man of middle age? Sometimes he is doing as much work, and perhaps more, than older people. The minimum salary should be $800. In the city of Montreal you cannot secure help unless you pay $2.50, $3 or $4 a day, and yet the Government starts those young men at $600.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: I heartily support the suggestion of the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy). The whole class should be increased very materially, and so far as the soldiers are concerned, the language used was very moderate. It is a shame that we should start them at such a low salary. There cannot be any salary paid commensurate with the sacrifices they have made. In whatever class they are put, it is the duty of this country to see that they commence at a proper salary.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext:
Evidently those gentlemen are talking for Hansard. As the Acting Minister of Finance has pointed out, an extra $200 may be added to the $600, and

that is more than many of the school 'teachers in this country are getting today. There are very few school teachers in the rural schools of Ontario, and they pay bigger salaries than the city schools, who are drawing more 'than $650 to-day.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman talking for Hansard,?

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext:
These stenographers who
start in after a three month's business course do not stop at $600. They are getting much better salaries than the school teachers of this country. The Toronto Globe, for instance, two or three months before last midsummer, carried two or three columns every day of advertisements for teachers, with a second class certificate, at ia salary of $500 to $700. I think we should leave it to the commission to decide each case on its .merits and if they think a man's training justifies them in granting an extra $200 he will receive it. A school teacher has to spend a much longer time in study than a stenographer, and paying her way during all that time.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: I do not put the returned soldier on the same basis as the civilian school teacher, -and I do not think it is right for the hon. gentleman to do so. When these men left this country to fight the battles of the Empire the whole country in an ebullition of popular feeling bade them Godspeed and a safe return, and promised that the country's last dollar would be spent in making them comfortable when they came home. Talk about school teachers! Why, one commission connected with the Trade Department of this Government got an Order in Council put through the other day to employ thirty-eight stenographers in Ottawa at $1,200 a year each. I 'think the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Blake) is a military man himself and did some good service, and surely he should stand up for his brother soldier and see that he gets treated in a decent way-I do not say in a generous way, but we should at least provide him with what a man ordinarily requires to live on. I am prepared to move that a special clause be inserted on page 17 limiting grade " G " of the second division to the returned soldier wlm has seen 'active service in France.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: What about other fronts ?

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext:
And on other fronts. 1 would not applythisprovieion to soldiers who have only been to England, although many of them may be deserving. I beg to move that a special clause be inserted limiting 
grade "C" of the second division to returned soldiers who have done duty overseas, except those who have remained in England, and that the minimum salary be $900 and the maximum $1,500, instead of $600 and $1,000 respectively.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: I would point out that by section 46 the maximum of this grade is increased by $200, compared with the salary under the old Act. I would also call attention to section 12.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: I do not think that is doing much for the soldier, when we remember that there is now a tax on tea and coffee' and that the price of bacon and all other articles of food has gone up. I am rather surprised that the Acting Minister of Finance takes that view. Section 12 does not grant an increase of $200; it only gives the commission power to grant it if they see fit. Now, I do not wish to see the returned soldier at the mercy even, of the Civil Service Commission, or of the minister or the deputy head; I would like to see this Parliament bold enough to toe the mark and say that the soldier has earned a decent wage, and we should make provision for him here in the Act.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: I rather like the idea of embodying the suggestion in the statute, because we all remember that at the outbreak of the war, with a view to inducing civil servants to join the colours, an Order in Council wias passed' promising civil servants who enlisted 'both their military and civil pay; but only a few weeks ago the Government cancelled that Order in Council and went back on the solemn pledge they gave to the men- who left Canada. I say it was a shame and dishonourable to break a solemn pledge in that way.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext:
It 'is true the commission have power to give an additional $200, but I do not like leaving it to the commission or even to the minister. I think Parliament should have courage enough to come forward boldly and say, "We want this thing arranged in this very way.'' The amount we are offering to the returned soldier is not large enough. The only positions that are open to him are messenger-ships and positions of that sort carrying only a small salary. Many of these returned soldiers were earning very mach^ bigger salaries before they left Canada, hut now through wounds or disablement they have to take these lower-salaried positions with $600 or $800 to start with. I would support an amendment that the minimum salary for the returned soldier be $1,000,

and that would only be carrying out to a very small extent the pledge we gave to these boys when they left our shores. Many of them to-day are walking the streets of our towns and cities because there are not enough positions to go around. I think we should redeem our pledge to them at least to the extent of giving them a minimum salary of SI,000, and I beg to move accordingly.
Mr. MAN30N: I would like to make a couple of points. One is in regard to what the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Blake) said. I notice in the House that whenever an hon. member takes' a stand in regard to keeping down expenses .somebody stands up and says that he is taking a whack at the returned soldier. I do not think that is playing the game. I do not . think that the hon. (memfber (for North Winnipeg took any whack in any shape or form at the returned soldier. I did not hear him say anything that reflected in any way upon the returned soldier. I happen to be a returned soldier myself and if he had said anything at which I could have taken offence I would have done so. This thing is being carried to an excess in this country. I .believe we are getting hysterical about people taking whacks .at returned soldiers. That is one point that I desire to make. The other point is this: I have sat in this House and heard a good many hon. members hitting at the soldier who has not got beyond England. I may speak upon that because I got beyond England myself. I wish to say, in justice to the man who has not got beyond England, that many good men have not got beyond England because they could not help themselves. After a man gets to England he is turned over to the overseas military authorities and he cannot say where he shall go. It took me seven months of hard work, breaking orders and ignoring rules in order to make myself so useless in England that I would >be sent to France. If I had not done that I would have stayed in England and been one of those despised men who stay in England. A great many of the men who stay in England do just as hard work as the majority of those who go to France. There are a great many men in France who are sixty miles behind the firing line and they are just as safe as if they were sitting in this House of Parliament.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: What about the longrange guns?	.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext:
They could shoot to England just as well as they . could shoot to
the bases in France. I think there should be a little more justice done by hon. members to the man who goes to England and who probably does his best to get to France but does not .succeed in getting across.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: This is a Civil Service Act and we .are basing the salaries in the Act upon the theory that we are merely creating a Civil Service. It is quite true that many of these positions should go to returned soldiers. But inevitably a great many of these positions will be filled by persons who are not returned soldiers. I would think that a iboy of fourteen ot fifteen who happened to be a messenger, packer or sorter and was getting $700 or $800, was doing very well indeed. True, that sum may not be a fair reward to the returned soldier of older age, and perhaps with a family. However, I do. not say that the suggestion is not worthy of consideration, but I want to point out that an amendment is not possible now to increase the minimum or maximum in that division. That would require a fresh resolution to be placed on the Order Paper, and it would have to be assented to by His Excellency the Governor General. I have no doubt that all these matters in reference to the returned soldiers will have to receive due consideration by the Government in the early future.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext:
There is no compulsion to force people into the Civil Service, and consequently I would not be in favour of having the minimum salary too low. But I do think that the amendment that was moved in regard to the returned soldier has something to justify it. We have heard a great deal about the returned soldier, the generous treatment that he has received, and should receive. We discussed that question earlier in connection with this Bill. The fact that the returned soldiers are not represented in the personnel of the commission justifies the criticism that is offered of this measure and the endeavour to provide all the safeguards that are necessary to ensure that they shall receive the treatment that they are entitled to. The hon. member for St. James (Mr. L. A. Lapointe) pointed out the difficulties that people living in large cities, such as Montreal, experienced in trying to live on less than $1,000 a year. When I heard the hon. gentleman make those remarks I could not help but think of all the people in this country who never see $1,000 from one year -s end to the other, and who are labouring

hard in order to secure a living for themselves and their families. That is particularly true of a certain class who are engaged in the public service. I refer to the rural mail carriers. These people have been taking contracts and delivering the mail year after year at a salary such as is not mentioned in the Civil Service list at all. I would just like to contrast the position of these public servants with that of the people who have a wall of protection all around them, whose hours of labour are regulated, who are superannuated in their old age and who receive much more generous treatment than those who are engaged in 'this branch of the public service to which I refer.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: Up to $1,200. Probably there will be very few returned soldiers who would care to accept a menial position at $800. But some soldiers with a pensiun of $600 or $700 or $800, might do very well with that amount of money. But if you throw the throttle open wide and say that the returned soldier must start in at $1,000 or $1,200, this country is going to feel it in the long run. We have got the taxes piling up at an enormous rate, and while I intend to see that justice is done to the returned soldier the representatives in this House have some other duties to perform. They have to see that this [DOT]country is protected. I appeal to hon. gentlemen. Sometimes I have said that I am pleased that I am growing old and will soon pass off this stage.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: I would ask hon. members to hear my reason. It is that I fear that we will have the cry dinned into us for the next fifteen, twenty or thirty years, nothing but the returned soldier. God bless the returned soldier, we will try to do justice to him, but let us be fair to the country itself, and let us not be swept off our feet by the voice of the demagogue constantly crying out, " The returned soldier!"

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: I cannot quite appreciate the minister's position in saying that we must have a special resolution before we can do what is proposed. I apprehend that the whole of section 46 is subject to amendment. If it is not so, I do not know where parliamentary practice comes in. Does the minister say we cannot knock out the whole clause if we like?

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext: A motion may be made to reduce expenditure, but a proposal which involves an increase must be initiated by a resolution, accompanied by the consent of the Governor General. My hon. friend will remember that this very Bill was introduced by a resolution, solely because it involved an expenditure of njoney.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext:
Very well, there is a very simple remedy. Let us take $1,000 off Grade A and another $500 off Grade B. Then we can raise the pay of the returned soldier from $900 to- $1,500. Then we will not commit a breach of the constitution.

My hon. friend is specious in his arguments, and if I may be allowed to use the expression, there appears to he subterfuge, to which my hon. friend is not prone. In regard to the hon. member for Springfie'd (Mr. Richardson) seeking to impugn other people's motives, I want to tell him, and tell you, Mr. Chairman, that I never was more earnest in anything in my life than when I rose to-night to try to do something if I could that would compel the Government to make decent provision for men who are back from the front. I know of men that are back here who, to use a slang phrase, are on their uppers. Many of them have not got the means to come to Ottawa, others who are here are out of employment, knocking at the door of the Government, and yet grumbling at the fact that the Government have nothing to offer them. I am no demagogue, Mr. Chairman, I want you to understand that when I take up a case of this kind I take it up from conscientious conviction. What I said ion a previous occasion is true, this Government has always been very prolific in its salaries to the " big guns " of the country. There is Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, who has drawn the sum of $17,500. There is Professor Macal-lum of Toronto University, the chairman of some scientific research committee, whom nobody has ever heard of, nobody knows what he has ever done, or what benefit he has been to the country, and yet he is getting the sum of $10,000. I read a list of salaries here the other night which ranged from $10,000 down to $6,000. Never a kick about that; but the moment a man stands up to make an ordinary plea, free from demagogism, for the returned soldier, he is met by a gentleman who shouts, "wolf, wolf!" I want to give the member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Blake) the credit for having done good service, and if that hon. gentleman had something said to him it was because he impugned other members' motives, and accused them of talking for Hansard. I do not have to talk for Hansard, Mr. Chairman, and I resent that sort of talk. I am going to move my amendment, and I am going to put it to the vote of the committee. I am going to move that the higher grade be reduced and that we raise grade C in the Third Division so that instead of being from $6Q0 to $1,200, it shall be from $1,000 to $1,500.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext:
The trouble with the Civil Service, as I understand the matter, is not the amount at which we start anybody, but the amount that we are paying those
who have been rendering efficient service to the public but are carried off into other avenues of employment. The difficulty has been the leakage from the Service of the good men at the top. It would be a terrible mistake, in my judgment, to attempt to reduce the salaries that are paid to those in the Civil Service, who, by their experience, their talents and by their faithful service, have earned higher and better stipends. Those are the men that we want to keep, but, unfortunately, they are continually leaving the public service, to be promptly engaged by private corporations. What inducement have you got to offer to a clever young university man? Is it the $600 salary at the bottom, or the $5,000 salary at the top. Never dream for a moment of reducing higher salaries, but rather increase them if possible so as to hold your good men. A salary of $600 is quite ample for messengers, porters, and employees of that class to start with, and they can climb to the $1,200 as in proposed clause. Some reference has been made to the Food Control Office, with which I happen to be connected, and some persons have talked about stenographers being paid $1,200 a year in that department. For us to set two scales of remuneration all through the different classes of the Civil Service or the public service, one scale for the civilian who has not been overseas and another scale for the soldier who returns from overseas, will create a condition that will not be for the good of the returned soldier. I am ready to go further and say, with the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson), that we are devoting too much of our time to a consideration of what the returned soldier is going to get when he enters the Civil Service. There will be four or five hundred thousand returned soldiers, and we cannot jam them all into the Civil Service. My opinion is that we shall be doing what is ultimately in the best interest of the returned soldier if we direct our attention more to getting him back into civil life in some position into which he can fit, and, if possible, in the work which he was doing before he went overseas, if we get into our mind that the Government have to find positions for all the returned soldiers, it is inevitable that we shall be trying to drive a lot of square plugs into round holes and vice versa, and we shall ultimately get the returned soldier into a position for which he will curse us. I am not afraid of being classed amongst those who are,-if you will permit me to use the term-batting the returned soldier. I am not advertising my feelings towards the returned soldier. They are just as genuine as those of any ether hon. member, and I am just as intensely interested in the men who are overseas. But I repeat: We are placing the returned soldier in a false and invidious position when we are constantly harping on the necessity of the Government putting him into some position for which he is not fitted. Let us, if we can, devote our attention to getting the returned soldiers back into the class of work for which they are fitted, getting it into their minds that the whole four or five hundred thousand soldiers cannot be put into this class of positions, and that if the country is to carry on, there must be a levelling up and getting the returned soldiers into the class

of work they can do. Any returned soldier in whom I am interested will never be urged by me to take a position under this or any other Government. I shall try to get him into a position for which he is fitted.

If possible, we should get him into the position in which he was before he went overseas, and we should get it into the heart and mind of the returned soldier that that is going to be his ultimate destiny and in his own interest. The worst thing that can happen to the returned soldier is the idea that we are going to pauperise them, and everything contained in the discussion that takes place in regard to the Government taking care of the returned soldier simply means that we are going to make wards or paupers of them as if they were not independent men.

speechtext:
I cannot let the remarks of the hon. member (Mr. G. B. Nicholson) pass without a word of protest. I am a returned soldier and a member of the Returned Soldiers' Association. I refrained from saying a word on the debate with reference to the returned soldier, because I thought the discussion was reaching limits that perhaps some of the hon. members who spoke would regret later on. Most of the hon. gentlemen who have opposed anything with respect to the returned soldier owe their seats in this House -to the returned soldier and to the soldier, and they should have regard to their electorate. Let us look at this question candidly and clearly. About a year ago the Government passed an Order in Council whereby all positions in the Civil Service were to go to returned soldiers, except in the case of men who were unfit for military service. At that time military service was for men between the ages of eighteen and forty-five. Since then there has been a change in the regulations, and only men in the first category are excluded from positions. The Government has settled that. Eighty or ninety per cent of the returned soldiers, after the war, will have just as sound and clear brains and will be physically as sound as my hon. friend, if not much more so. They will not be looking for Government jobs. They -will not be and are not the parties that we can put into the Civil Service. The men who desire to be put into the Civil Service are those poor unfortunates who have been disabled, many of whom have left situations carrying salaries of four or five thousand dollars a year-and I know a number who are older than the hon. gentleman, who left good positions and went to the war, and many of whom are still serving in the war. I know men of sixty years of age who left good positions in which they were drawing $3,000 or $4,000 a year, and who have been serving in the trenches constantly day and night since they went overseas. In many cases those men come home wounded, and their wounds and injuries are of such a character that they are unable on their return to take up the positions that they previously occupied. I know one man, for instance, who used to earn a large salary as a moulder. He has only about one-quarter of a lung left owing to German gas. I know a man who was a surveyor on railway construction work, a man of high attainments. One of his legs is now one and one-half inches shorter than it formerly was and the other is two and oneJhalf inches shorter, so that he is lame and unable to go around. This man must seek some other occupation because he could not take the same place as he had before. The idea of the Government, and that of anyone who has in his heart a soft spot for the returned soldier, is that the Civil Service shall be for those men whose efficiency has been impaired. Hon. members say that a civil servant should be one hundred per cent efficient. Thi* returned soldier is unafble to take up hia old posi-

tion and he is only efficient to tlhe extent of 'forty or fifty per cent. A returned soldier may have lost an arm, but still he may be capable of filling a position at a desk in the Civil Service and doing his duties just as *well a,s a man who has all his limbs and faculties. It is those men for whom we want positions, not for returned soldiers like my robust hon. friend from Fort William (Mr. Manion), who has just returned from the front.
We must get the injured man a position, and his wife and family must be looked after, and no man to-day can look after himself, let alone a family, on much less than $1,000 a year. I think it is only right that we should raise the minimum salary for the .soldier. I do not want to give details, but I know of sad cases of soldiers with large families to look after who have been disabled by service at the front and have had to take positions in the Civil Service at $600 a year, and that is the limit that pretty nearly all of them are getting. To that is added a pension of $150 or $200 a year, or $600 if the man is totally disabled. No matter what' a man's attainments might be, if he has .served as a private he only' gets a portion of a private's full pay when he is disabled. I say he must have something beyond that pension, and while I do not want to be considered as making a raid upon the treasury on behalf of the returned soldier, when the next election comes they may be able to look after themselves and possibly attend 'to those who have looked after them, but in the meantime when we are dealing with an Act that is .supposed to do something for the returned soldier we should see to it that he gets the first call for the higher-salaried positions as well as the lower. If you are going to give the returned soldier a position, give him -a salary that he can live on and bring up his family, a salary that will not keep him in a state of continuous poverty. This country ought to be ashamed of itself. I saw a list to-night of about two hundred names of men who have been, in the public service for years, many of them in the city of Toronto in the Customs, Inland Revenue, and other departments, none of whom had ever got more than $800 or $900 a year. That used to be a fortune thirty years ago, and it was a large sum before the war, but things have moved very swiftly since and everything has gone up in price; wheat is now three and four times the price it was before the war. We must meet the situation in some way. I repeat,
I do not want to raid the treasury; I do 
not want more than is fair and right for the returned 'soldier; but I do not want to hear the returned soldier reviled in this House and told he has no more rights than the ordinary member of a labour union. I say that he has more than the member of a labour union. I know where the attack on the returned soldier eomes from and we will attend to that when the proper time comes. I say it ill becomes any man who sits in this House as a returned soldier's candidate, a man who has received the votes of returned soldiers, to 'Stand up and say they have no rights and should have no privileges, that they should toe pauperized, and that they have no special privileges coming to them more than to the ordinary individual. I trust we have heard enough on this subject, and I almost feel inclined to say to. the minister, let us pass on to the next order of business, and by the time the Bill is ready for its third reading the minister may have thought out a way of meeting the situation.

I am not going to permit the hon. member to insinuate that I reviled the returned soldier or that I said he was not worthy of tlhe same treatment as a member of a labour union. I can tell the hon. member and all other members of this House that I am quite willing to have the returned soldiers and the soldiers overseas judge me by the manner in which I have treated them. I have stood on the floor of this House and said what I have said because I feel we are not doing the best for the returned soldier or for any other soldier when we undertake to set up such a standard: as the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) would set up by his amendment, whereby the returned soldier would be given a position at a higher rate of wages than the man who is working alongside of him. The returned 'soldier does not want that. If the salary of the civil servant is nof sufficiently high for the .returned soldier, that is an entirely different question.
Mr. 'EDWARDS: The hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) after dealing with this question, to his own satisfaction, suggested the advisability of passing on to another item. This is not the first time he has thought in this House that everything had been said on a question when he had concluded his speech. There are others, however, who. hold views on this matter, and while 1 was not privileged to be in the House this afternoon when this matter was being discussed, I have been

here since eight o'clock and I have heard nothing said that could 'be construed toy any person whose brain was in normal condition of health to be an attack on the returned soldier. As a member of this House who recognizes hie responsibility to his constituents, I believe that every member of this House, whether or not it has been his privilege to tread the soil of France and do his part overseas-and that is a great privilege in my estimation-and whether sitting to the right or the left of the Chair, is desirous of doing his duty to the returned soldier and giving him more than a fair share. I had understood, since the Government made their announcement that the returned soldier was to get the preference in appointments to the Civil Service, that we had to take into consideration the man's fitness for the position that was vacant. I had understood that if the returned soldier was qualified for the position, he unquestionably would have the preference over every other person, and I have not heard any person in this House or outside question the wisdom and correctness of that view. I believe the judgment of hon. members of this House is that the returned soldieT shall be given the preference for the higher-salaried positions as well as the lower if he possesses the necessary qualifications. But how can any person logically maintain that we must leave out of consideration the qualifications of the applicant for the position? How can any man who recognizes his responsibility to the people-and we must certainly recognize that responsibility when we appoint a man to a position in the Civil Service- agree to the appointment of a man to the Civil Service just because he is a returned soldier, regardless of his fitness for the position? The proposal strikes me as absolutely illogical and indefensible. First of all, the returned soldier must possess the qualifications- necessary to fill the position that is vacant, and if he possesses those qualifications I am in the judgment of every member of this House when I say that he should be given preference over any man who has not been overseas. I did not understand the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) to say anything different from that, nor do I believe the hon. member for North Simcoe was justified in the attack he made on the hon. member for East Algoma.
In regard to this question of salaries, last session when the question of salaries in a certain department of the Government wias uip for consideration the principle was laid down, by the granting of a bonus of a
certain amount, that this bonus ishoiuld apply to men whose salaries were under $1,000 a year and not to men whose salaries were over $1,000 a year. If that was a correct principle last session why should it not be a correct principle this ;session? It meant that the Government recognized that men cannot maintain their families on less than $1,000 a year. If that was true last year it is just as true this year. I agree with much that has been said with regard to the salaries of the higher officers in the Civil Service. A man who- has been for years in the service of the Government, who- has shown his fitness for the position that he occupies, I believe, is entitled to look forward to a gradual increase in his salary, according to his years of service, always having regard to his fitness to discharge the duties of the office he holds. I cannot understand the justice or fairness of telling a man who happens to be in one division that he is thereby excluded, notwithstanding his merit, from passing up to another division.
There is another feature of this salary question that properly comes in here. I do not know whether it is because there are several thousand civil servants in Ottawa or not, but ever since I have had the honour of a seat in this House, that is since 1908, periodically the question of salaries affecting people in the Civil Service in Ottawa has come before the House and it has always been just a little before an election. But there has been no consideration given-and I want the full emphasis to be placed upon the word "no"-to the salaries of the people in the Outside Service. Not only has there been no consideration given to the salaries of the people in the Outside Service but in many places it is impossible to get the least bit of encouragement when the matter is brought to the attention of the various departments of the Government. Let us take the case of the country postmaster; all his time is taken up by his duties, which begin at half past six in the morning and continue until nine o'clock and often till ten in the evening. He can not engage in any other occupation as he is in the service of the Government or the service of the country. If he is in the service of the country, why should he not receive consideration for the -service which he renders? In a village in my own county there is a postmaster whose total remuneration, allowing for rent and everything, amounted last year to $870. That means that he is expected to give faithful service to the people of this country in the

position he occupies and maintain his family on $800. Members come .here year after year and session after session and consider the rights of the civil servants in the city of Ottawa. Why? Because the civil servants of the city of Ottawa number several thousand and they can back up their demands with their solid vote. That is the reason why. Because these people in outlying country districts are only scattered voters here and there and have no particular voting strength when the election comes on, their claim is ignored. In considering this matter I want to tell you another thing. While every hon. member of this House has a right to state what he considers is a proper salary for a civil servant, is it not right that every member should protest against men in high places deliberately stealing from the treasury of this country and putting the money in their own pockets? Deliberated stealing-what else do you call it? A specific vote of $2,500 is granted to him for the purpose of paying his expenses when he goes over to Great Britain to attend the sessions of the Privy Council. In. connection with the statement made by the Acting Minister of Finance that the Civil Service Commission will carry out an investigation during the recess with a view to the reorganization and classification of the service, and for the purpose of removing any inequalities, I desire to express my pleasure that a member
of the commission is here this evening. There are two glaring inequalities which require to be removed. One of them is in connection with the salary of $10,000 paid to a gentleman referred to earlier in the evening by the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy). His appointment and continuance in office is nothing less than a public scandal. This man is paid $10,000 a year 'for doing absolutely nothing of benefit to the people. My information is that the desire to get rid of him was so strong in Toronto University that they were at their wits' end to know where to dump him, and they finally dumped him upon this Government. I have been trying since the beginning of the session to ascertain what this gentleman does, and I can now tell this committee that he does nothing of any public benefit. I would suggest to the minister, and through hion to the commission, that one of the first acts of the commission should be to put an end both to the job and to the salary. That is one inequality. Another inequality, just as farcical as showing the way public business is conducted in this country, will be found in another department of the Government. The commission will find a man in charge of 150 employees; they will find that man disbursing $12,000 per month as the pay-roll in that branch; they will find this man and these 150 employees handling and controlling, if my memory serves me correctly, over $30,000,000 in a year. Yet the man in charge of that branch gets the munificent salary of $1,800 per annum. That is as big a farce and as great a scandal as is the case of the ten-thousand-dollar-a-year man at the other end of the line. The -CHAIRMAN: By consent of the committee we revert to section 30. The member fer Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) has moved that the following be substituted as section 30:
30. -Subject to the provisions of section three of this Act, the power to remove or dismiss any deputy head, officer, clerk or employee, shall vest in the -Commission.
Before exercising such power, the Commission shall require a statement in writing, from the minister in the case of a deputy head, and from the deputy head in all other cases, giving the causes, reasons and facts invoked for such dismissal.
Upon receipt of such statement in writing the Commission shall forthwith oomm-unicate a copy of same to the deputy -head or other employee whose dismissal is sought.

subtopic: AND TO BRING THE OUTSIDE SERVICE UNDER ITS PROVISIONS.
speechtext:
I have already explained what I intend by this amendment. The power of appointment is, by the change that we made this afternoon, now vested in the commission. In section 42, subsection 3, we inserted the word " appoint " instead of the word " supply." We have, therefore, vested the appointing power in the commission, and I do not see why we should not vest the dismissing power in the commission. I do not desire to see an employee dismissed summarily; neither do I wish to see a man subject to any arbitrary action from any superior, and that is the reason why I have put in my amendment that he whose dismissal is sought shall have the -right to know the reasons why the charges are made against him and the facts that are brought to justify his dismissal, and that he shall have the right within three days to file a statement in writing. My -attention was called to the fact that three days was too short a time, because some Civil -Service employees are quite a distance from here, -say at the Coast. I am, therefore, willing that " three weeks " or " twenty days should -be inserted instead of three days. Within that period the employee has a right to answer the charges or justify himself in writing. Should the employee -fail to write within the time limit, the commission, to whom the file is sent, may proceed ex parte and take into consideration the report and act upon it. If the object of this Bill is to do away with patronage, this amendment should carry. Patronage is exercised not in appointments only; the worst kind of patronage is exercised in dismissals. This Act has for its purpose to make the service efficient, to employ the best men and to make them feel they are going to be treated in the proper way by Parliament and by the commissioners, this amendment is just to protect them fro-m any idea they -may have that they may be

arbitrarily dealt with by deputy heads, or heads of departments, or any other party under whose control they may be. It is only fair that a man who is going to lose his bread and butter, who is charged with an offence or misconduct for which he is subject to dismissal, should at the very least have an opportunity of stating his case, so that hereafter if anybody should desire to look into the matter, there will not be only one side of it, tout we shall be able to judge the case on its merits having heard both sides. I put this as a test whether the Government are really in earnest in bringing down this measure. If they want to do away with patronage, so far as positions are concerned, leaving 12 m. aside the other part of patronage which has been called to the attention of the committee toy my hon. friend from North Winnipeg (Mr. Blake), the power of appointment and the power of dismissal ought to rest with the: same authority, and he who is to (be dismissed ought at least to have the right to put his case -before the 'body which is to decide as to his fate.

speechtext:
The amendment of my hon. friend from Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) ought to be accepted. The power of dismissal is just as important, indeed, I 
think' it is more important and more dangerous, than the power of appointment so far as political interference or patronage is concerned. Parliament has always considered that to be so. In fact, when this Parliament wants to place a public official or servant above political patronage and to be sure of his impartiality, it enacts that the official cannot be dismissed by the Governor in Council, and that only a vote of the two Houses of Parliament can dismiss him. It so enacts in the case of judges, the Auditor General, the Civil Service Commissioners and other officers. It happens that the Governor in Council is entitled to appoint gentlemen to certain offices, but that the authority which makes the appointment has no power to dismiss those officers. Under the Bill as it stands, we are legislating in the opposite direction. The Governor in Council would be deprived of the power of making appointments, but would have the right to dismiss the officers it has not right to appoint. If the Government wants to do away altogether with the plague of patronage and political interference it should accept the amendment of my hon. friend; the Civil Service Commission should be empowered to make the dismissals -as well as the appointments, and the Governor in Council should not interfere.

It would, I think, be rather peculiar if the Crown delegated that power to any other body.

speechtext:
By a method of selection established by an Act of Parliament, the commission does select appointees to the Civil Service, but once they are appointed they are the servants and employees of the Crown, and the Crown should reserve the right of dismissal. There is no doubt that in the past, in the case of political 'appointments, the power of dismissal was abused by governments, but hon. gentlemen know that related almost entirely to the Outside Service. I never heard anybody complain about improper dismissals by the Government so far as the Inside Service is. concerned, where appointments are made upon competitive ex-

animation and promotion depends upon merit. If dismissals have been improperly made from the Inside Service by the Crown in the past I do not know of any such case. Dismissals have been made, however, for cause. I hope that when the same principle which obtains in the Inside * Service is applied to the Outside Service-appointment after competitive examination, and promotion upon merit-there will be no dismissals by the Government except for cause. I do not feel that the amendment should be accepted, and I trust that my hon. friend will not press it.

subtopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.

speechtext: On the Order being called for the second reading of Bill No. 70, to consolidate and amend the Railway Act-(Hon. J. D. Reid):

subtopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Surely the second reading is not going to be pressed on the House now. I was told in the lobby this evening that my hon. friends opposite had prepared for an all-night session by organizing relief squads.

subtopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Order, order.

subtopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Why "Order"? We are not going to be treated like slaves. That is what I was told, and I have reason to believe it is true.

subtopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I have no desire to go on with the Bill to-night if there is any objection.

subtopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: There is objection.

subtopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I thought we might
get into committee and make a start on the Bill, but if there is objection I will not press the second reading.

subtopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
There is no objection.
I object to the principle of certain clauses.

subtopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I would like to state
here that my hon. friend is entirely in error in stating there was any organization on this side of the House to keep this *thing going all night by relief squads. Whoever told my hon. friend that was drawing on .his imagination, because no such thing was plannell.

subtopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
If I am in error, I am
glad to acknowledge it. I hope I shall not have again to refer to the same point.

subtopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT.

subsubtopic: ANN OUN C BMBN T MADE BY HON. MR.
speechtext:
I may perhaps
be out of order but I cannot resist the temptation of informing the committee that a press despatch has been received stating that Hon. Dr. Beland has been released and is coming home.

subtopic: RELEASE OF HON. DR. BELAND, M.P.
subsubtopic: ANN OUN C BMBN T MADE BY HON. MR.
speechtext:
Three cheers for Dr.
Beland.
Hon. members rose, gave three cheers for Dr. Beland, and sang " For He's a Jolly Good Fellow."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: RELEASE OF HON. DR. BELAND, M.P.
subsubtopic: ANN OUN C BMBN T MADE BY HON. MR.
speechtext:
I have received a cablegram from Sir George Perley with respect to Hon. Dr. Beland's release, which reads:	.
London, May 13th, 1918.
The Prime Minister,
Ottawa.
Have telegram from Beland at Rotterdam saying he has been released from Germany Am personally delighted, and am sure this news will be most welcome to you and all other Canadians.
Perley.
Following the reading of the cablegram, hon. members rose in their seats, and cheered.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: RELEASE OF HON. DR. BELAND, M.P.
subsubtopic: ANN OUN C BMBN T MADE BY HON. MR.
speechtext: I might add that I communicated to my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, three days ago, I think, the news that Dr. Beland's release was likely to take place, but we were under injunction to say nothing about it in public. I am very glad that the anticipation then conveyed to us has now been fulfilled. All of us who know Dr. Beland have the very highest appreciation of his character, of his ability and of his services as a public man. We have all been greatly distressed by the fact that he has been detained so long in Germany and has endured such hardships, and there is none who will not join, as we have joined just now, in the most warm recognition of the fact that he has been set at liberty.

subtopic: RELEASE OF HON. DR. BELAND, M.P.
subsubtopic: ANN OUN C BMBN T MADE BY HON. MR.
speechtext:
In justice to the right hon. the Prime Minister and to Sir George 
Perley, I might add that 6ince the internment of our dear colleague, Dr. Beland, the Prime Minister and the Government have done their utmost to have him released.
On the motion of Hon. A. K. Maclean the House adjourned at 12.17 a.m. Tuesday.
Tuesday, May 14, 1918.
